content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes the use of a Random Forest classifier-head on top of a pretrained backbone to deal with the few-shot image classification problem. Additionally, the method exploit ensembling to boost the classification accuracy. Results on miniImageNet and CIFAR-fs are provided to show the effectiveness of the proposed solution.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
--------

- The method looks at the few-shot learning problem from a different angle, using a Random Forest approach, which makes it stand out from recent work.

- The way the Random Forest classifier is trained (via difference vectors) is interesting and it could be exploited in other methods.


Weaknesses
----------

1) I am not sure what are the elements of novelty in this work. The authors should explicitly mention upfront in the introduction what are the main contributions. The use of an encoder trained with standard epoch training is not new. A variety of recent state-of-the-art methods used this approach, e.g. see Big-Transfer (BiT, Kolesnikov et al. 2020), LITE (Bronskill et al. 2021), and the simple baseline of Tian et al (2020). The use of an ensemble is also not particular new. The only element of novelty seems to be the use of a Random Forest head, but the empirical results are not convincing (see points below) and I am not sure this approach has any clear benefit.

2) There is no evidence that the proposed SimForest classifier is more effective than alternative approaches. The method works by creating difference vectors of support-query pairs and assigns a positive label if they belong to the same class. This reduces to a binary classification problem, which could be solved by any other classification approach. Convincing baselines should be provided to show that given the same setup, other approaches are less effective. For instance, a simple linear head or an MLP could be used to replace the forest on this binary task. Table 4 (appendix) seems related to what I am talking about here, showing that using a a 3-layer MLP is in practice more effective than using the Random Forest, supporting my observation. Moreover, previous work suggests that a simple linear head can be fine-tuned on top a pretrained model without the need of using difference vectors with solid results (Tian et al. 2020).

3) The claim that SimForest is faster than other approaches (e.g. mentioned in Section 6) is not substantiated by data. To support this claim the authors should report the Multiply-Accumulate operations (MACs) and the inference time on a given task for SimForest and the other baselines. This should include the entire pipeline, e.g. the time spent aggregating the difference vectors.

4) Empirical results are not convincing. If I read this correctly, Table 1 reports the results of using SimForest as part of an ensemble with another method. However, the baseline results obtained by the method on its own (top row) are significantly lower than all the others. Only when the method is used in an ensemble the results gets better. The comparison does not seem fair. The table should include additional baselines, e.g. an ensemble of other methods (excluding SimForest) to see if adding SimForest to the ensemble (in place of another method) gives any clear benefit. In other words, ensembling ProtoNes+RelationNet could be as effective as ensembling Protonet+SimForest but this is not showed in the table.

5) Additional experiments. The experimental section shows results on miniImageNet and CIFAR-fs that start to be obsolete. Recent work has focused on much more challenging benchmarks, such as MetaDataset (Triantafillou et al. 2019) and VTAB (Zhai et al. 2019). Additionally, recent state-of-the-art methods can scale to large images and much deeper architectures (e.g. see Big-Transfer). The method does not seems to have any major scalability issue, therefore I recommend to try the pretrained backbones provided in the Big-Transfer repository and test the model on VTAB and MetaDataset with large images.

6) Minor corrections. The paper uses the word "plug-in" in various sections (including the abstract) but often this seems misleading, the word "ensemble" seems more appropriate.


References
----------

Bronskill, J., Massiceti, D., Patacchiola, M., Hofmann, K., Nowozin, S., & Turner, R. (2021). Memory efficient meta-learning with large images. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 34, 24327-24339.

Kolesnikov, A., Beyer, L., Zhai, X., Puigcerver, J., Yung, J., Gelly, S., & Houlsby, N. (2020, August). Big transfer (bit): General visual representation learning. In European conference on computer vision (pp. 491-507). Springer, Cham.

Tian, Y., Wang, Y., Krishnan, D., Tenenbaum, J. B., & Isola, P. (2020, August). Rethinking few-shot image classification: a good embedding is all you need?. In European Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 266-282). Springer, Cham.

Triantafillou, E., Zhu, T., Dumoulin, V., Lamblin, P., Evci, U., Xu, K., ... & Larochelle, H. (2019). Meta-dataset: A dataset of datasets for learning to learn from few examples. arXiv preprint arXiv:1903.03096.

Zhai, X., Puigcerver, J., Kolesnikov, A., Ruyssen, P., Riquelme, C., Lucic, M., ... & Houlsby, N. (2019). A large-scale study of representation learning with the visual task adaptation benchmark. arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.04867.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper lists the following challenges in few-shot learning:

1. High variance and bias due to insufficient supervision.
2. Insufficient representation complexity due to the smaller model size favored by episodic training. 
3. Computational cost.

To solve the challenges, the authors propose using an ensemble-based solution with an additional predictor constructed by epoch-trained feature extractor + forest-based classifier, and present performance improvements.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper discussed several challenges of few-shot learning and suggests ensemble as a potential solution. 
While I believe ensemble can certainly improve few-shot learning, I have the following concerns regarding the presentation, method, and experiment of this paper.  

**Claims**
In the introduction, the authors make several claims regarding few-shot learning. While most of them are supported by published papers like (Wang et al., 2020), I expect more evidence to support them. For example:

- *approximations of the few-shot predictors becoming unreliable with high potential bias and variance*

Do the authors mean that few-shot learning models always demonstrate high prediction bias and variance simultaneously? In my opinion, the insufficient supervision problem of few-shot learning is more associated with high variance and low bias situations. 

 - *Secondly, computational problems arise when a learning algorithm tends to get stuck in a local minimums.*

I expect the authors to elaborate more on this point. I cannot see a direct connection between computation and optimization. 

- *While resnet-18 is infeasible as an encoder for episodic training*

The 'infeasible' makes this a wrong claim. It is certainly feasible to use resnet-18 and even larger models like WRN in few-shot classification with episofic training. I suggest the author refer to (https://fewshot.org/miniimagenet.html) for comprehensive performance comparisons with different model architectures including WRN-28-10, densenet, and even ViT.

**Method**

1. While I agree ensemble should be able to improve few-shot classification, I don't see a clear reason in this paper why the proposed simforest method is indispensable for a successful ensemble. Specifically, what are the advantages of this method over ensembling multiple different few-shot classification models? A comprehensive discussion on different ways of ensembling (e.g. same method different networks, same network different random seeds, epoch training + episodic training) is expected to support the effectiveness of the proposed method. 

2. As the proposed method is purely based on ensemble, I personally disagree to call this method a 'plug-in'. In my opinion, a plug-in should be a method that improves upon existing methods like [1]. Otherwise, any ensemble can be called a 'plug-in'.

3. I cannot see clear support for why adopting the forest-based prediction head. 
The author discusses *In addition, to minimize the extra computation cost of ensemble, we choose a non-deep classifier for SimForest. With pretrained features, the random forest classifier in SimForest can complete the classifier training within a few seconds.* 
However, 'within a few seconds' for obtaining a classifier-given extracted features is by no means computationally efficient in my opinion. They are certainly other alternatives like closed-formed classifiers (e.g., ridge regression, kernel ridge regression), linear layer + few-step gradient descents (like proto-MAML in [2]). 

**Experiments**

Since this paper is more positioned as a generic 'plug-in' method, I expect to see more comprehensive experiments including: 

1. More model architectures beyond Conv4 and ResNet12.

2. Challenging settings such as cross-domain few-shot learning (e.g., miniImagenet -> CUB).

3. larger scale experiments with MetaDataset [2]. 

The current experiments with miniImageNet and CIFAR are only the most basic ones. 

[1] Free Lunch for Few-shot Learning: Distribution Calibration.

[2] A Dataset of Datasets for Learning to Learn from Few Examples.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
My concerns regarding the clarity of the discussions and novelty are listed in the previous question. 
The proposed method demonstrates insufficient novelty and the discussions are not clear and convincing enough. 
I do not notice significant reproducibility issues.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In my opinion, this paper does not meet the standards of publishing at ICLR due to:

1. Unsupported, insufficiently discussed, and wrong claims.

2. Unclear or unsupported motivations for the proposed method. 

3. Severely insufficient experiments.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an efficient classifier that can be attached to the internal feature representation of a pretrained classification model to facilitate better few-shot learning. The classifier is a decision forest that estimates the degree to which two images (or image sets, for k-shot learning) have the same label. The experimental results show that ensembling the proposed method with other few-shot methods improves the latter's performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The proposed method is simple, and widely applicable. It can be combined with existing pretraining strategies and few-shot methods, and the paper shows that (for some setups) the addition of the method to various existing methods performs better than those existing methods alone.

I did not understand why the particular way of featurizing the image pairs was chosen. E.g. why absolute feature differences and not just feature differences?

The comparisons between the different methods seem to reveal that (1) SimForest alone does not perform as well as the existing methods, and (2) for an existing method X, SimForest ensembled with X fares better than either SimForest or X. This seems to suggest that perhaps the power of the method lies in ensembling rather than the specifics of SimForest. Could it be that ensembling two SOTA few-shot methods sets the new state of the art? The paper itself seems to suggest that SimForest is not the best choice, by showing that an MLP performs even better.

Side note -- one aspect I did not see in the paper is the discussion of the inference cost, as a function of the number of classes to choose amongst. For example, FS methods that compute representations and then compare those using the Euclidean distance benefit from the efficient computation of the latter as well as, potentially, efficient approximate nearest-neighbor methods. Does SimForest offer an efficient way to compute distances, ideally one that is compatible with modern accelerators?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is mostly clear, though some choices (the use of absolute feature differences) did not seem to be clearly explained. The term "absolute vector difference" should be clearly defined -- it took some hunting to determine that it did indeed mean the per-dimension absolute differences, as opposed to e.g. the Euclidean distance between vectors. The paper uses the term "epoch training" which I think I understand the meaning of but the term should be well defined.

The results are on mini-imagenet and cifar-fs -- I believe this is not sufficient, especially as multiple other standard FS datasets exist.

The novelty of the approach is limited in my opinion. The use of pretrained representations on which a classifier is trained is common, and the use of a decision forest specifically is a small enough change (if it is novel) and, according to the paper itself, not the optimal choice. The evaluation appears to demonstrate the (well recognized) power of ensembling more than that of SimForest.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a simple method for improving few-shot learning when it is ensembled with other methods. However. the proposed method is not shown to be the optimal choice, and important ablations (such as the results of ensembling other methods with each other) are not given. I do not think it meets the bar for ICLR.

content.title: SimForest:  An Efficient Plug-in to Boost Few-Shot Learning Performance
content.TL;DR: We develop an efficient (i.e:  computation-efficient, convenient, universally adaptable) ensemble method which can significantly boost the performance of varioius few-shot learning algorithms.
content.abstract: Due to a lack of labeled training data and the subsequent unreliability in empirical risk minimization, few-shot learning algorithms usually suffer from high variance and bias in their predictions.  Ensemble, on the other hand, combines predictions from multiple predictors, thus alleviating the aforementioned unreliability. Essentially, we believe that ensemble is a simple yet effective solution to tackle the core problems in few-shot learning; therefore, we develop a plug-in (ensemble) method to boost the performance of trained few-shot models. To maximize the performance of ensemble, we use epoch-training to develop the feature representations used in the plug-in; in contrast, episodic training is used to obtain the feature representations of the original few-shot models. To minimize the extra computation cost induced by ensemble, we adopt a non-deep classifier (e.g: random forest) for the plug-in, which can complete its training within a few seconds. Our method achieves substantial improvements for the few-shot learning, consistently outperforming all the baseline methods.
